\paragraph{Within-$\alpha$ sensitivity at $\alpha{=}1.0$.}
Table~\ref{tab:threshold_sensitivity} reports the predictive cessation outcome under five entropy-drop thresholds (5\%--25\%) at $\alpha{=}1.0$ (Pythia-410M, seed~42).
All five thresholds produce identical outcomes: token entropy drops 40.7\% at generation~1, far exceeding even the most conservative threshold (25\%), so every threshold triggers at the same generation.
The intervention conclusion---peak perplexity 57.0, recovery in one generation, final perplexity 21.3---is invariant to threshold choice within this range.

\begin{table}[h]
\centering
\small
\caption{Threshold sensitivity at $\alpha{=}1.0$ (Pythia-410M, s42, fp32). All thresholds trigger at generation~1 (entropy drop 40.7\%$\gg$threshold), producing identical recovery trajectories.}
\label{tab:threshold_sensitivity}
\begin{tabular}{rccr}
\toprule
Threshold & Trigger gen & Peak PPL & Final PPL \\
\midrule
5\%  & 1 & 56.99 & 21.29 \\
10\% & 1 & 56.99 & 21.29 \\
15\% & 1 & 56.99 & 21.29 \\
20\% & 1 & 56.99 & 21.29 \\
25\% & 1 & 56.99 & 21.29 \\
\bottomrule
\end{tabular}
\end{table}

\paragraph{Cross-$\alpha$ operating band.}
The within-$\alpha$ analysis establishes threshold invariance at $\alpha{=}1.0$ but does not address whether thresholds generalize across contamination levels.
We examine observed entropy trajectories from the alpha sweep (not actual intervention experiments at $\alpha{<}1.0$) to characterize the operating band.
The maximum entropy drop across 10 generations varies by contamination level: 7.5\% at $\alpha{=}0.0$ (fine-tuning drift only), 7.7\% at $\alpha{=}0.10$, 7.8\% at $\alpha{=}0.25$, 22.4\% at $\alpha{=}0.50$, 35.3\% at $\alpha{=}0.75$, and 62.1\% at $\alpha{=}1.0$.
Thresholds below 7.5\% (e.g., 5\%) trigger on clean training data---a false alarm.
Thresholds above 22.4\% (e.g., 25\%) miss $\alpha{=}0.50$, the lowest contamination level with meaningful entropy signal.
The safe operating band is therefore $[10\%, 22\%]$: any threshold in this range produces zero false alarms on $\alpha{=}0.0$ while detecting contamination at $\alpha{\geq}0.50$.
The reported 15\% threshold sits near the center of this band.
This analysis is based on entropy trajectories from non-intervention training runs; whether actual intervention at $\alpha{<}1.0$ would produce the same triggering behavior remains unvalidated.

\section{Mutual Information Analysis}
\label{app:mi_analysis}

We estimate the Gaussian mutual information lower bound between token entropy (canary) and each diversity metric across contamination levels, using $T{=}11$ data points per series ($T{=}10$ for two conditions).
The Gaussian estimator $\hat{I}_G = -\frac{1}{2}\log_2(1 - r^2)$, where $r$ is the Pearson correlation, provides a conservative lower bound on MI; we do not report KSG nonparametric estimates due to uncorrected positive bias at $T{=}11$.
The $\alpha{=}0.05$ data point is excluded because it uses an experiment excluded from the dose-response analysis.

Table~\ref{tab:mi_bounds} reports the mean Gaussian MI across the three distinct-$n$ metrics for each $\alpha$ level.
MI follows a V-shaped curve: it drops from 0.112~bits at $\alpha{=}0.10$ to a minimum of 0.010~bits at $\alpha{=}0.25$, then rises monotonically to 0.270~bits at $\alpha{=}0.75$.
MI remains positive throughout the blind zone ($\alpha \leq 0.45$; range 0.010--0.141~bits), confirming that canary--diversity coupling exists below the detection threshold but falls below PermG's statistical power floor at $T{=}10$.
There is no discontinuity at $\alpha_c \approx 0.50$: the detection onset reflects power accumulation, not an abrupt change in information coupling.
Bootstrap 95\% CIs span 1--3 orders of magnitude at $T{=}11$, so individual point estimates should be interpreted cautiously.

\begin{table}[h]
\centering
\small
\caption{Gaussian MI lower bound (bits) between token entropy and distinct-$n$ diversity metrics ($T{=}11$, Pythia-410M, fp32). Mean across distinct-1/2/3; $\alpha{=}0.05$ excluded (see text). CIs omitted due to width at $T{=}11$.}
\label{tab:mi_bounds}
\begin{tabular}{rrc}
\toprule
$\alpha$ & Seeds & MI (bits) \\
\midrule
0.10 & 2 & 0.112 \\
0.25 & 3 & 0.010 \\
0.30 & 1 & 0.062 \\
0.35 & 1 & 0.098 \\
0.40 & 1 & 0.119 \\
0.45 & 2 & 0.141 \\
0.50 & 3 & 0.107 \\
0.60 & 2 & 0.209 \\
0.75 & 1 & 0.270 \\
\bottomrule
\end{tabular}
\end{table}


\subsection{Partial Correlation Analysis}
\label{app:partial_corr}

To distinguish genuine canary$\to$diversity temporal structure from shared-trend confounding, we compute partial correlations controlling for generation number $t$ (Table~\ref{tab:partial_corr}).
For each canary--downstream pair, we report (i)~contemporaneous correlations (same generation) and (ii)~lagged correlations (canary at $t{-}1$, downstream at $t$), in both zero-order and partial (controlling for $t$) forms.
All results aggregate 18 pairs per $\alpha$ level (3 seeds $\times$ 2 canaries $\times$ 3 diversity metrics; $T{=}11$ observations per series).

\begin{table}[h]
\centering
\small
\caption{Partial correlation analysis controlling for generation number. Contemporaneous: canary$_t$ vs downstream$_t$; Lagged: canary$_{t-1}$ vs downstream$_t$. Zero-order: raw Pearson; Partial: controlling for generation $t$. Sig.: pairs with $p{<}0.05$ out of 18. Negative $\Delta$ indicates partial $|r|$ \emph{exceeds} zero-order (trend removal strengthens the association).}
\label{tab:partial_corr}
\resizebox{\columnwidth}{!}{%
\begin{tabular}{@{}l cc cc cc cc@{}}
\toprule
& \multicolumn{4}{c}{Contemporaneous} & \multicolumn{4}{c}{Lagged (canary$_{t-1}$)} \\
\cmidrule(lr){2-5} \cmidrule(lr){6-9}
& \multicolumn{2}{c}{Zero-order} & \multicolumn{2}{c}{Partial} & \multicolumn{2}{c}{Zero-order} & \multicolumn{2}{c}{Partial} \\
\cmidrule(lr){2-3} \cmidrule(lr){4-5} \cmidrule(lr){6-7} \cmidrule(lr){8-9}
$\alpha$ & $\bar{|r|}$ & Sig. & $\bar{|r|}$ & Sig. & $\bar{|r|}$ & Sig. & $\bar{|r|}$ & Sig. \\
\midrule
0.00 & 0.414 & 3/18 & 0.323 & 0/18 & 0.563 & 8/18 & 0.524 & 9/18 \\
0.50 & 0.590 & 9/18 & 0.381 & 2/18 & 0.759 & 12/18 & 0.841 & 17/18 \\
0.75 & 0.636 & 9/18 & 0.521 & 3/18 & 0.831 & 17/18 & 0.913 & 18/18 \\
\bottomrule
\end{tabular}}
\end{table}

Two patterns emerge.
First, contemporaneous partial correlations drop substantially relative to zero-order ($\bar{|r|}$: $0.590 \to 0.381$ at $\alpha{=}0.50$), and significance collapses from 9/18 to 2/18, confirming that much of the same-generation association is attributable to shared generational trend.
Second, lagged partial correlations \emph{increase} relative to zero-order ($\bar{|r|}$: $0.759 \to 0.841$ at $\alpha{=}0.50$; $0.831 \to 0.913$ at $\alpha{=}0.75$), with 35/36 detection-condition pairs retaining significance.
Removing the shared trend strengthens the one-generation canary lead, confirming that the lag-one structure reflects genuine temporal precedence rather than co-trending.
At $\alpha{=}0.00$ (null control), lagged partial correlations are weaker ($\bar{|r|}{=}0.524$) with mixed significance (9/18), consistent with fine-tuning drift producing some spurious lag associations but no systematic pattern.

\section{Discussion}\label{sec:discussion}

\paragraph{Scope and failure modes.}
Our Granger-precedence claim is scoped to temporal predictive improvement~\citep{granger1969investigating,shojaie2022granger}: bivariate tests cannot exclude confounders, and the FPR CI ($[2.1\%, 17.9\%]$) means Type~I error may be non-negligible.
Four of fifteen cross-architecture conditions do not confirm forward detection (\S\ref{sec:generalization}), each isolating a distinct PermG assumption violation: precision sensitivity (GPT-2 bf16), seed dependence (Pythia-1.4B), and entropy decoupling (SmolLM3-3B).
These patterns require architecture-specific null calibration before deployment (Appendix~\ref{app:extended_discussion}).

\paragraph{Granger causality limitations.}
Our observation sequences ($T{=}10$--$25$) are far shorter than econometric standards ($T{\geq}100$); permutation testing avoids asymptotic assumptions but cannot recover power lost to short samples~\citep{shojaie2022granger}.
Bivariate tests are susceptible to omitted variable bias; first-differencing removes shared linear trends but nonlinear confounds remain possible.
PermG tests linear precedence only; transfer entropy (Appendix~\ref{app:transfer_entropy}) yields 0/192 significant pairs, consistent with either absent nonlinear structure or insufficient short-$T$ power.
Partial correlation controlling for generation number confirms that canary$\to$diversity lag-one structure persists after trend removal (35/36 pairs significant; Appendix~\ref{app:partial_corr}).

\paragraph{The $\alpha{=}0.60$ non-monotonic anomaly.}
The detection gap at $\alpha{=}0.60$ affects all direction-checked methods (PermG 0/8, threshold 0/8, Toda--Yamamoto 1/8), while bidirectional DiffXCorr maintains detection (6/8), suggesting temporal lag compression defeats directional separation.
PermG recovers to 5/8 at $T{=}25$, consistent with $\sqrt{T}$ power scaling restoring detection as additional observations disambiguate synchronous from lagged responses.

\section{Conclusion}\label{sec:conclusion}

Method choice alone shifts null-control FPR from 7.4\% to 94.4\%, establishing that single-method analyses cannot reliably distinguish temporal precedence from artifacts.
PermG, the lowest-FPR method (7.4\%, 9~seeds), yields token entropy one-generation-ahead precedence over diversity collapse (24/24 forward, 0/24 reverse at $\alpha{=}1.0$; ${\geq}6/8$ in 11/15 cross-architecture conditions).
The blind zone below $\alpha_c$ constrains practical deployment to settings with sufficient contamination; evaluation at ${>}$7B parameters remains open.

\section{Conclusion}
\label{sec:conclusion}

Lead-lag analysis in iterative training collapse is far more fragile than the current literature assumes.
Method choice alone inflates spurious-signal rates to at least 62.5\%, first-differencing exposes canary$\to$perplexity associations as entirely spurious, and regime dependence causes the same Granger test to shift from 24/24 to 0/8 significant pairs across contamination levels.
These design considerations establish that single-method, single-regime analyses (the current default) cannot reliably distinguish genuine temporal precedence from statistical artifacts.

Our systematic five-method comparison through the Multi-Method Consensus Test (MMCT) identifies permutation Granger causality as the recommended detection method: it combines the lowest null-control FPR among all five methods (7.4\%, 4/54 across 9 seeds; 7/9 seeds yield 0~FP) with high sensitivity, exhibiting a steep dose-response onset from 0/8 (blind spot, $\alpha{\leq}0.45$) to 6/8 ($\alpha{=}0.50$; sigmoid $k{=}15.7$, ${\approx}3{\times}$ steeper than smooth-signal predictions) with reliable detection at $\alpha{\geq}0.75$.
The other four methods each fail in characteristic ways: naive cross-correlation inflates FPR to 75\%, differenced cross-correlation cannot separate forward from reverse precedence, threshold onset is power-limited at $T{=}10$ under $3\sigma$ calibration, and Toda--Yamamoto Granger provides supplementary detection at reduced power (directional assignment under verification).

Applying permutation Granger, token entropy exhibits robust one-generation-ahead precedence over diversity collapse at $\alpha{=}1.0$ on WikiText-103 (24/24 forward, 0/24 reverse across 4~seeds, replicated on GPT-2-medium and OPT-1.3B), with cross-architecture validation confirming forward detection (${\geq}6/8$) in 11 of 15 model-seed combinations spanning five families (345M--6.9B); non-confirming conditions span precision sensitivity (GPT-2 bf16), seed dependence (Pythia-1.4B), entropy decoupling (SmolLM3), and bidirectional confounding (GPT-2 s43).
Directional asymmetry is domain-dependent: consistent unidirectionality holds on WikiText across all regimes, while C4 exhibits near-symmetric bidirectional coupling at $\alpha{=}0.50$ (PermG reverse 7/8), though forward detection remains robust in both domains.
This finding is deliberately scoped to lexical diversity, not model collapse broadly, since the perplexity channel proved entirely spurious under differencing.

The design considerations we expose arise from generic properties of short, non-stationary time series.
Cross-architecture (five families, 345M--6.9B), cross-scale ($3.4\times$ within Pythia), and cross-domain (C4) validation confirms that both the design considerations and the method recommendation are not specific to a single experimental configuration; evaluation on models at ${>}$7B parameters remains an open direction.
Limitations are detailed in \S\ref{sec:limitations}; future directions are discussed in \S\ref{sec:discussion}.

\section{Introduction}
\label{sec:introduction}

When language models train iteratively on their own output, the training distribution progressively loses its tail modes, a phenomenon termed model collapse~\citep{shumailov2024curse,alemohammad2024mad}.
This process can be triggered by vanishingly small synthetic fractions~\citep{dohmatob2025strong}: lexical diversity narrows, calibration deteriorates, and each generation inherits the biases of its predecessors.
As machine-generated text grows prevalent on the web, such feedback loops pose a growing risk to production pipelines, and by the time standard quality metrics register degradation, the distribution may have already shifted irreversibly.

This threat motivates a fundamental question: \emph{can we reliably detect the onset of model collapse?}
The answer is less clear than it might appear.
Iterative training produces short, noisy time series (often fewer than 15 points) where detection power drops sharply~\citep{boettiger2012limits}, and model collapse is a first-order transition~\citep{truong2026phase}, structurally ruling out the critical-slowing-down early-warning signals that ecologists rely on~\citep{scheffer2009early} (\S\ref{sec:related_work}).
More fundamentally, no prior work has systematically compared detection methods on this problem; as we show, the choice of statistical test alone can shift conclusions from universal detection to complete null on identical data.

\begin{figure*}[!t]
\centering
\includegraphics[width=0.92\textwidth]{figures/fig_composite_hero.pdf}
\caption{Detection landscape overview (Pythia-410M, fp32, PermG).
\textbf{(a)}~Phase diagram: FDR-significant canary$\to$diversity pairs across $\alpha$ and $T$; dashed curve: fitted $\alpha_c(T) \propto T^{-\gamma}$; $\diamond$: non-monotonic anomaly; $\star$: dissolution at $T{=}25$.
\textbf{(b)}~Dose-response with sigmoid fit ($\alpha_c{=}0.483$); regime bands mark blind, onset, sync-dip, and detection zones.
\textbf{(c)}~Method sensitivity: five methods on identical data; PermG achieves 0\% null-control FPR with 75\% detection at $\alpha{\geq}0.50$.
\textbf{(d)}~Cross-architecture validation ($\alpha{=}1.0$): forward detection (${\geq}6/8$) in 11/15 conditions spanning five families (345M--6.9B).}
\label{fig:hero}
\end{figure*}

We systematically map this landscape on Pythia-410M~\citep{biderman2023pythia} across 13 contamination levels with multi-seed replication (Figure~\ref{fig:hero}).
Our most consequential finding concerns method sensitivity: five statistical methods applied to identical data yield null-control FPR spanning 7\% to 94\% ($\kappa{=}0.185$; Figure~\ref{fig:hero}c), demonstrating that single-method analyses cannot reliably distinguish real signals from artifacts.
Permutation Granger causality (PermG), the lowest-FPR method (7.4\%, CI $[2.1\%, 17.9\%]$, 9~seeds), reveals structured terrain rather than smooth degradation: detection is absent through $\alpha{=}0.45$, then jumps from 0/8 to 6/8 significant pairs within a 2-percentage-point interval (Figure~\ref{fig:hero}a), before a non-monotonic dip and eventual reliable detection above a power-law boundary $\alpha_c(T)$ (Eq.~\ref{eq:alpha-c-theory}).
Cross-architecture evaluation at $\alpha{=}1.0$ across five families (345M--6.9B) supports forward detection in 11/15 conditions, with four non-confirming cases isolating distinct failure modes (\S\ref{sec:generalization}).
Our canary claim is scoped to diversity metrics (distinct-$n$~\citep{li2016diversity}); Granger precedence establishes temporal predictive improvement, not causation (\S\ref{sec:method}).

Our contributions are:
\begin{enumerate}
    \item \textbf{We document method sensitivity as a primary finding} (\S\ref{sec:mmct}).
    Five methods yield null-control FPR from 7\% to 94\% ($\kappa{=}0.185$); PermG, the lowest-FPR method across all five (7.4\%, CI $[2.1\%, 17.9\%]$, 9~seeds), is selected as the primary detector.

    \item \textbf{We map the detectability landscape} of iterative model collapse (\S\ref{sec:regime}--\ref{sec:dose_response}).
    Detection is absent through $\alpha{=}0.45$, then jumps from 0/8 to 6/8 within 2 percentage points; a detection boundary consistent with power-law scaling $\alpha_c(T) \propto T^{-\gamma}$ ($\gamma \in [0.64, 2.08]$; Eq.~\ref{eq:alpha-c-theory}) organizes three confirmed regimes (blind, onset, detection) plus one unexplained non-monotonic anomaly.

    \item \textbf{We empirically validate a cascade ordering for canary metric selection} (\S\ref{sec:cascade}).
    Under mode amplification, entropy responds before diversity by ${\geq}1$ generation (Principles~\ref{thm:entropy_leads}--\ref{prop:div_lag}), confirmed in 14/15 experiments ($\alpha \geq 0.30$; GPT-2-medium s43 bidirectional).
\end{enumerate}
